content: Acute leukemia is a malignancy that originates in the bone marrow, specifically affecting myeloid and lymphoblastic precursor cells. These hematopoietic cells are poorly differentiated and exhibit rapid proliferation. As a result, their accumulation disrupts the bone marrow's ability to produce normal blood cells. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) are life-threatening diseases that, if left untreated, will inevitably result in death. In most cases, the underlying cause of these leukemias is not apparent. However, in some instances, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) has been implicated. A Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE) is essential to identify patients who require immediate intervention. This evaluation is critical in both AML and ALL to ensure timely management. The diagnostic criteria for AML and ALL share similarities. According to the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, the presence of 20% or more blasts in a bone marrow biopsy or peripheral blood smear is diagnostic for AML. However, certain genetic abnormalities, such as inv(16), t(16;16), t(8;21), and t(15;17), are diagnostic for AML even if the blast percentage is below 20%. For ALL, the diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of 20% or more leukemic lymphoblasts in a bone marrow aspirate or biopsy. In the pretreatment assessment of AML, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing must be performed for all cases. Additionally, seven days after the completion of the induction phase of chemotherapy (commonly referred to as the 7+3 regimen), a bone marrow biopsy is required to evaluate the remission status. Certain precautions must be observed during the diagnostic and treatment process. For instance, if a patient with AML has a coagulopathy disorder and is at risk of bleeding, a lumbar puncture should not be performed until the coagulopathy is corrected. Furthermore, chemotherapy agents with cardiotoxic potential should not be administered without first assessing cardiac symptoms and performing an echocardiogram.
